error.message: name must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$ without leading '.' or any '..'

BadRequest.description: Validation failure; error.code disambiguates (invalid_name, invalid_path, unknown_project, project_path_missing, path_and_project, bad_request).

OriginForbidden.description: Cross-origin request on a mutating route.

UnsupportedMediaType.description: POST body was not declared application/json.

code.description: Stable machine-readable code from the registry in the top-level description. Clients switch on this, never on message.

features.description: Capability strings from the registry in the top-level description. Clients MUST ignore unknown entries and MUST feature-detect anything beyond the ttyd-compatible core before using it — this list is the only cross-repo skew defense that exists.

hostname.description: Short hostname, as bin/wt shows in its menu header (bin/wt:63).

terminalPath.description: Absolute path of the start command (WT_PICKER).

user.description: The service user — whose shell every terminal hands out.

exists.description: Whether path is currently a directory. False warns that bin/wt would silently fall back to $HOME (bin/wt:46,82) and the API would refuse with project_path_missing.

Session.description: One dtach session, observed from the filesystem. Field derivations and their failure modes are specified in session-lifecycle.md.

attached.description: True while someone is looking at this session. That sentence is the contract; the derivation below is not, and it has already changed once. Clients MUST NOT read the socket mode themselves. Since `scrollback-replay` shipped, wtd holds its own dtach attachment to each deep-linked session in order to buffer its output, which pins the socket's owner-execute bit on permanently — so the bit that used to answer this means nothing for such a session. Three signals, first match wins: (1) wtd's own count of WebSocket clients for the session; (2) dtach clients in /proc that are not wtd's own held attachment — someone attached over SSH or from the bash menu, which no other signal can see; (3) for a session no hub holds, the execute bit exactly as before (`srwx------` attached, `srw-------` idle).

createdAt.description: Socket file mtime, RFC 3339 UTC. In practice this is creation time; nothing observed mutates a dtach socket's mtime after bind (session-lifecycle.md notes the caveat).

cwd.description: Current working directory of the session's shell (the dtach master's direct child), read live from /proc/<pid>/cwd — it moves when the user cd's. Null when unresolvable.

name.description: Socket basename minus `.sock`. Deliberately unconstrained: the bash menu creates names the POST rules would reject (e.g. containing spaces), and this API must list every session the menu can see — the two pickers must never disagree about what exists.

pid.description: PID of the session's shell (the dtach master's direct child — the process whose cwd is reported), not the dtach master itself; the master is plumbing. Null when unresolvable.

SessionCreateRequest.description: `path` and `project` are mutually exclusive; omitting both means the service user's $HOME. Unknown extra properties are ignored (a newer client against an older server degrades predictably; capability discovery is /api/v1/meta's job, not schema strictness here).

name.description: Stricter than the bash menu on purpose — see POST description for why each rule exists (leading dot: invisible to the menu's glob; `..`: unreachable by deep link).

path.description: Absolute directory to start the shell in. Must exist and be a directory; must not contain bytes < 0x20 or 0x7F (they cannot be safely single-quoted into the `bash -c "cd ...; exec bash"` command line the parity rule requires, so they are rejected rather than escaped heroically).

info.description:
## Security model — read before adding anything

This service fronts a **writable, unauthenticated shell** running as the service
user. There is **no authentication at any layer of this API, by design** — access
control is the network interface the daemon binds to (a tailnet IP, `127.0.0.1`,
or a specific interface; wtd refuses `0.0.0.0`/`::` even when explicitly
configured). Every endpoint below is reachable by anyone who can reach the port.
The question for any change to this file: *does it widen who can reach the shell?*

## CSRF and cross-origin policy (normative for every route)

Because there is no auth, the classic CSRF mitigations-by-credential do not exist;
any web page a user visits can attempt requests against a tailnet IP. Therefore:

- **Mutating routes** (`POST`, `DELETE`) reject any request carrying an `Origin`
  header whose authority (host[:port]) differs from the request's `Host`
  authority → `403` with code `origin_forbidden`. Non-browser clients (the iOS
  app's URLSession) send no Origin header and are unaffected; wtd's own picker
  pages are same-origin and pass. Reverse proxies must preserve the original
  `Host` header or this check will reject legitimate browsers.
- **`POST` routes** additionally require `Content-Type: application/json`
  → `415` with code `unsupported_media_type` otherwise. HTML forms cannot send
  `application/json`, which kills form-based CSRF outright.
- wtd **never** sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` — or any CORS headers at
  all on `/api/*`. CORS headers exist to *grant* cross-origin access; this API
  must never grant it.
- Request bodies are capped at 16 KiB → `413` with code `payload_too_large`.
- The same Origin policy applies to the `/ws` upgrade itself — see
  `ws-protocol.md` section 12; a cross-site WebSocket is a cross-site shell.

Residual exposure, stated honestly: the Origin-vs-Host comparison stops ordinary
cross-site requests (Origin names the attacker's site, Host names this server —
mismatch, rejected). It does **not** stop DNS rebinding, where the victim's
browser requests `http://attacker-hostname:7681/...` after the attacker's DNS
flips to this IP — then Origin and Host both name the attacker's hostname, they
match each other, and the check passes, `/ws` included. The only complete fix is
validating `Host` against an allowlist; a `WT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` config key is
reserved for that and deliberately **not** in v1, because unconfigured it would
break tailnet MagicDNS names and raw-IP access, and a misconfigured allowlist
locks the owner out of their own box. What contains rebinding meanwhile is the
precondition it needs: the victim's *browser* must itself be on the private
network this daemon binds to. That is the repo's standing security stance — the
service is exactly as private as the interface it binds to — restated, not
weakened.

## Path behavior outside this spec

- `GET /` serves HTML: with no `?arg=` query parameter, the **browser session
  picker** (lists dtach sessions, links to `/?arg=<name>`); with `?arg=` present
  (even empty), the **terminal page**, whose script opens
  `ws://<host>/ws + location.search` exactly as ttyd's bundled client does. Pages
  use relative URLs so they work behind a path-stripping reverse proxy.
- `GET /ws` is the terminal WebSocket — the entire contract is
  `ws-protocol.md`. It appears below only as a stub so the path is not "free".
- Unknown paths → `404` with the standard error object. Known paths with wrong
  methods → `405`, code `method_not_allowed`.
- All `/api/*` and `/token` responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store`.

## Error object

Every non-2xx response from `/token`, `/healthz`, and `/api/*` is the `Error`
schema: `{"error": {"code": "...", "message": "...", "detail": "..."}}`. `code`
is a stable machine-readable string from the registry below (clients switch on
`code`, never on `message`); `message` is one human-readable sentence; `detail`
is optional elaboration. The registry is open-ended — clients MUST treat unknown
codes as opaque failures of the given HTTP status.

| code | HTTP | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `bad_request` | 400 | Body is not a JSON object, or violates the schema in a way not covered below. |
| `invalid_name` | 400 | Session name fails the create-side rules (see POST /api/v1/sessions). |
| `invalid_path` | 400 | `path` is not absolute, contains control bytes, does not exist, or is not a directory. |
| `unknown_project` | 400 | `project` names no entry in the projects file. |
| `project_path_missing` | 400 | Project exists but its path does not (the bash picker would silently fall back to `$HOME`; the API refuses to guess). |
| `path_and_project` | 400 | Both `path` and `project` were supplied; they are mutually exclusive. |
| `already_exists` | 409 | A live session with this name already exists. |
| `not_found` | 404 | No such session / no such route. |
| `origin_forbidden` | 403 | Cross-origin request on a mutating route (or the /ws upgrade). |
| `unsupported_media_type` | 415 | POST without `Content-Type: application/json`. |
| `payload_too_large` | 413 | Body over 16 KiB. |
| `method_not_allowed` | 405 | Known path, wrong method. |
| `internal` | 500 | Unexpected server fault; `detail` says what, socket state untouched unless stated. |

## Features registry (`GET /api/v1/meta`)

The `features` array is the **anti-skew mechanism** between this repo and the iOS
client: the two repos share no CI, no type checking, and installed phone builds
do not update when the server does. A client MUST feature-detect any capability
beyond the ttyd-compatible core (`/`, `/ws`, `/token`) by checking this list, and
MUST ignore feature strings it does not recognize.

| feature | meaning |
|---|---|
| `token` | `GET /token` served (ttyd compat). |
| `url-arg` | `?arg=` is appended to the start command argv (always on in wtd). |
| `writable` | Terminal input is accepted (always on in wtd; ttyd `-W`). |
| `sessions-api` | `GET/POST /api/v1/sessions`, `DELETE /api/v1/sessions/{name}`. |
| `projects-api` | `GET /api/v1/projects`. |
| `picker-ui` | `GET /` serves the HTML picker when no `?arg=` is present. |
| `scrollback-replay` | A named (`?arg=`) connection is sent the session's recent output on attach, before live output. Implies `attached` is derived from wtd's client count, not the socket mode. |

Reserved for the future (a server advertising one implements its spec revision):
`auth-basic`, `base-path`, `tls`, `flow-control`.
info.summary: Browser terminal daemon: ttyd-wire-compatible WebSocket terminal plus a JSON API over dtach sessions.
info.title: wtd HTTP API

get.description:
HTML, not API. Without `arg`: the browser session picker. With `arg` (even
empty): the terminal page, which forwards its full query string to `/ws` —
preserving ttyd's client behavior so `http://host:7681/?arg=demo` exercises
the same `$1` code path in `bin/wt` that the iOS app's `sessionArg` uses.

parameters.description: Session name to deep-link. Validation happens in bin/wt, not here — a malformed name renders the picker (graceful fallback), never an error.
parameters.name: arg

get.summary: Browser picker (no ?arg=) or terminal page (?arg= present)

get.description:
The anti-skew endpoint (see the features registry in the top-level
description). Clients cache this per connection at most — it is cheap, and
the whole point is detecting a server that changed underneath an installed
client.

The `name path` shortcuts from the projects file (`WT_PROJECTS`, same file
and same parsing as bin/wt:30-37: first whitespace-delimited token is the
name, the remainder is the path; blank lines and `#` comments ignored). Each
entry reports `exists` — whether the path is currently a directory — because
`bin/wt` silently substitutes `$HOME` when it is not (bin/wt:46,82), and a
client should be able to warn before creating a session somewhere
unexpected. An absent or unreadable projects file is an empty list, not an
error, matching the picker (bin/wt:32).

Enumerates `$WT_DIR/*.sock` with the same visibility rules as `bin/wt`'s
`sessions()` (bin/wt:52-55): socket files only, dotfiles excluded (bash
globs skip them, so the menu cannot see them — the API must not disagree
with the menu about what exists). Names are the basename minus `.sock`,
sorted ascending by byte value.

Two rules that follow from "the two pickers must not disagree":

1. **Looser names than the API would create are still listed.** The bash
   menu accepts almost any typed name (bin/wt:80-83); a session named
   `my proj` must appear here even though POST would reject it.
2. **Stale sockets are reaped, not listed.** A socket whose master is gone
   (`connect()` → `ECONNREFUSED`) is a phantom — the menu lists it but
   attach fails. This endpoint verifies liveness and unlinks confirmed-stale
   sockets during the scan, converging both pickers on the truth. Yes, that
   mutates on GET; see session-lifecycle.md ("Reaping") for why that is the
   least-bad option and the re-stat guard against racing a concurrent
   `dtach -A` self-heal.

post.description:
Creates a dtach session **without attaching** — the API-side equivalent of
the picker's `n)` flow, for clients that want to prepare a session before
deep-linking into it.

**Parity is mandatory** (session-lifecycle.md, "Creation parity"): the exact
invocation is `dtach -n $WT_DIR/<name>.sock -z -r winch bash -c "cd <quoted-path>; exec bash"`
with `WT=1` exported — identical flags and command shape to bin/wt:26,47,83.
A session made here must be indistinguishable from one made in the menu;
in particular, missing `WT=1` makes any login shell using
docs/bashrc-snippet.sh auto-launch tmux inside the session (recursion — the
exact failure the variable exists to prevent, bin/wt:21-23).

Working directory resolution: `project` (looked up in the projects file) or
`path` (absolute, must exist), else the service user's `$HOME`. `path` and
`project` are mutually exclusive. Where `bin/wt` silently falls back to
`$HOME` on a missing directory (bin/wt:46,82 — right for a human at a menu),
the API returns an error — a program should be told, not guessed for.

Name rules are **stricter than the menu's**, deliberately:
`^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, plus MUST NOT start with `.` and MUST NOT contain
`..`. Each carve-out closes a real disagreement between surfaces:
a leading dot is invisible to the menu's glob (bash skips dotfiles,
bin/wt:54) — the API would create a session the menu cannot show; a name
containing `..` is rejected by the deep-link path (bin/wt:44) — the API
would create a session a saved iOS profile can never reach.

If the name matches a **stale** socket (master dead, connect refused), the
stale socket is reaped first and creation proceeds — same self-heal the
deep-link path gets from `dtach -A` (verified: dtach 0.9 recreates over a
stale socket).

Location.description: Canonical resource path for the new session.

409.description: A live session with this name already exists (a concurrent create loses the `dtach -n` bind race and also lands here).

delete.description:
Terminates the session's process tree and removes its socket, in the strict
ordering defined in session-lifecycle.md ("Cleanup ordering") — child first,
master observes and unlinks, unlink-by-wtd only as the verified last resort.
Ordering matters because each wrong order creates a distinct phantom:
unlink-first orphans a running invisible session; kill-master-first (SIGKILL)
leaves both a stale socket and an orphaned shell (both verified live).

**No path is ever constructed from `{name}`.** wtd enumerates the socket
directory and byte-compares `{name}` (URL-decoded) against the real entries'
derived names. This is why there is no validation pattern on this parameter:
the menu creates looser names than POST accepts, and those sessions must be
deletable too. A name that matches no entry is simply `not_found` — including
anything containing `/`, which can never match a directory entry.

Deleting a **stale** socket (master already dead) succeeds: the phantom is
verified via `connect()` and unlinked → `204`. Deleting an **attached**
session is allowed and kills the live shell under whoever is attached; their
dtach client exits and `bin/wt`'s menu loop survives and redraws
(bin/wt:15-16 — no `set -e` — and bin/wt:58-59). The API does not try to
guess whether that is what you meant.

parameters.description: Exact session name (basename minus `.sock`), URL-encoded as needed. Matched byte-exact against directory enumeration; never interpolated into a filesystem path.
parameters.name: name

204.description: Session terminated (or stale socket reaped) and socket gone.

404.description: No socket with this name exists.

500.description: Termination did not complete within the bounded escalation (session-lifecycle.md). The socket is left untouched — wtd never unlinks a socket it has not verified dead.

delete.summary: Terminate a session and clean up its socket

get.description: Plain-text liveness for systemd, scripts, and humans with curl. Returns `ok` when the HTTP listener is serving. It deliberately checks nothing deeper — dtach sessions and the picker binary belong to per-connection behavior, and a health check that can fail for reasons a restart will not fix trains people to ignore it.

The machine-readable contract, served by the binary that implements it so a client (or a person with curl) can inspect exactly what this build speaks. Rendered from api/openapi.yaml at build time; the served document and the repo file must not drift.

Exists solely because clients of ttyd expect it: the iOS app GETs it on every
connect, ignores failures, and sends the result as the handshake `AuthToken`
(Networking/TtydConnection.swift:174-190). wtd has no auth, so the token is
the constant empty string, matching ttyd 1.7.4 run without `-c` (verified
ground truth). Serving it keeps connect logs clean and third-party
ttyd-compatible clients working.

Not an HTTP resource in any REST sense — this path upgrades to the ttyd
`tty`-subprotocol WebSocket. The complete normative contract (upgrade rules,
Origin policy, handshake including the text-vs-binary frame trap, opcode
framing, resize semantics, ping/liveness, close codes, failure modes) is
`api/ws-protocol.md`. `?arg=` values are appended to the start command argv.

101.description: Switching Protocols; subprotocol `tty` echoed when offered.

400.description: Not a valid upgrade, or subprotocols offered without `tty`.

servers.description: wtd's single listener. host is the resolved bind address (a tailnet IP, 127.0.0.1, or an interface address — never a wildcard); 7681 is also the iOS client's default port (Models/ServerProfile.swift:7), so changing it means every beta user edits their profile.
